messages.subject: transposing data?
messages.body_plain:
Since this went so well last time...new question!

I'm trying to make a wide df from a long one, and I've been reading through the Specter chapters, trying all sorts of things, and can't seem to do what I want to do.

Here's the head of the df:

   PlotID Species.Code X.Cover
1 A-1-001       CASSPP     0.5
2 A-1-001        LOTSP     0.5
3 A-1-001        ARTTRI     0.5
4 A-1-001       ERIWRI     0.5
5 A-1-001       ERICON     0.5
6 A-1-001       PINJEF    15.0

I have 113 more plots, each with a different number of species that each have their own observation of percent cover. I would like to end up with a df that has one row for each plot, one column for each spp, and the X.Cover (%cover) values in the appropriate cells. 0s or NAs are fine for plots where a spp doesn't occur.

Each species (there are 337) is not listed for each plot, so there are no 0s already, if that matters.

I've tried various table(), melt(), cast(), unstack(), and some reshape(), but I still can't figure out how to do what I want to do. Any ideas?

Thanks!

library(tidyr)
df_long = data.frame(plot=rep(1:3, each=3), species=rep(letters[1:3], 3),

df_wide = spread(df_long, species, cover)
df_wide

spread "spreads out" the species column into separate columns by value.

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: transposing data?
messages.body_plain:
This implies that there are duplicate observations. That is, the same value for both plot and species in multiple rows. The error means that, since you have not specified what to do with duplicate values, dcast defaults to counting the number of observations. Look for any cells in the output that are 2 or greater - this should point you to the duplicate rows. If you want to sum or average duplicate rows, add the argument fun.aggregate=sum or fun.aggregate=mean to the dcast function call.
​

messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: if then syntax
messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

This sounds like you need ifelse(), a vectorized if else statement.

Some sample data:

> x <- rbinom(10, 1, 0.4)
> x
 [1] 1 0 1 1 1 0 0 0 1 0
> y <- runif(10)
> y
 [1] 0.3800851 0.8145238 0.9528767 0.7491175 0.8735943 0.7262976 0.1235017
 [8] 0.7678490 0.1400231 0.2878240

> ifelse(x, y+1, y-1)
 [1]  1.3800851 -0.1854762  1.9528767  1.7491175  1.8735943 -0.2737024
 [7] -0.8764983 -0.2321510  1.1400231 -0.7121760

Here I juse is ifelse(x, ...) because x == 1 isn't necessary with 0 and 1s because these are coerced to TRUE and FALSE.

The second arguments are the vectors (of same length!) for when the first argument is TRUE and FALSE, respectively.

HTH,
Vince

messages.subject: Pattern identification
messages.body_plain:
Good afternoon....

I'm running a sizable number of clustering operations. In particular, the KMeans and PAM cluster algorithms are somewhat path dependent depending on the seed values used for selecting their starting centroid/medioids. As a result I can get multiple different responses if I don't fix my seed values. And, as it happens, I'm finding that there can be substantial differences in the resulting clusters that result in some of those solutions being more useful to me than others.

Is there a good way given a list of (for example) 100 vectors each with cluster membership of each sample point to identify the set of unique solutions and how many times that solution was arrived at?

This is complicated by there being no guarantee that even given the "same solution" that the clusters will be identified the same way. i.e. in vector A and vector B which both grouped the same samples together into a cluster with the same members, in A that cluster might be cluster #1 and in B cluster #2.

I'm more of a python programmer by practice, and I'd do it in python by looping through all of the vectors, and replace the first cluster in the vector with another name (like "A") and propagate that change through the entirety of that vector for every member of that cluster, and then do the same with the second and so on with "B", "C"... Then I'd be able to compare them directly in a doable if ugly looping structure.

I have a suspicion that R should be able to handle this in a more elegant fashion. Suggestions are very welcome.

Nate

messages.body_plain:
I haven't used the party package for CART before, but it sounds like you are making a "tree" without any branches. I think you can use the "controls" argument to change the sensativity of your tree to make it more likely to branch. You may not have a significant relationship between your response variable and any of your predictor variables. The tree will stop branching as soon as it can no longer reject the null hypothesis. You can change your p-value with the "mincriterion" argument within the "controls" argument. (see ctree_control) in the documentation. You can also change the test type from "Bonferroni" to "MonteCarlo".

I have used rpart for CART analyses in the past, and found it pretty straightforward. It is more likely to give you a tree with way more branches than you know what to do with and you have to trim them down rather than trying to get them to branch more.

Hope that helps
Rosie

Hey, folks,

Thanks for the help, but Vince is correct. Your solution is close, but doesn't handle the label switch case very well. Is there an upcoming R user group session that I could use to demo the challenge since I think that'll be more effective than trying to describe it textually?

Here's the code I'm playing with at the moment. Basically what it does is read in a set of demographic data from csv, iterate through seed values 1:100 conducing Kmeans clustering, and saving the outputs to a list. It then implements Noam's suggestion, and appends the resulting unique vectors to the shapefile. In this case it comes up with 53 unique vectors, though quite a few are permutations of the label switch issue. Finally it joins the items together and writes it out to a shapefile.

I'm not particularly elegant with my R yet, so I also welcome stylistic suggestions.

Thank you,
Nate

# Load libraries
library(psych)
library(nFactors)
library(plyr)

#Kmeans function
kmeanscluster <- function(seed,indf,numclus,maxiters){
  set.seed(seed)
  fit <- kmeans(indf, numclus,iter.max=maxiters)
  aggregate(indf,by=list(fit$cluster),FUN=mean)
  return(fit$cluster)
}

# Read in the table
tracts <-read.table("walk_bike.csv",header=TRUE, sep=",",colClasses=c("character",rep("numeric",11)))
# Select just the fields to use for the clustering
natracts <-na.omit(tracts)
wtracts <-natracts[c(2:11)]
geoids <- natracts[c(1)]
colnames(geoids) <- c("GEOID10")

# Run Kmeans, no factor analysis
seeds <- 1:100
t <- lapply(seeds,kmeanscluster,indf=wtracts,4, maxiters=20)
# Prep for join to Shapefile
seeds_df <- data.frame(do.call("cbind",t))
colnames(seeds_df) <-c(paste("sd_",seeds,sep=""))
seeds_df <- data.frame(geoids,seeds_df)

# Noam's code
sets = laply(t, function(x) {

  uniques = unique(x)                  # This block renames the
  ints = 1:length(uniques)             # characters so they are in ascending
                                       # alphabetical order
  names(ints) = uniques

  fixed = ints[x]

  return(paste(fixed, collapse= " "))  # This collapses each vector into a string
})

# Tally up the unique strings

counts = table(sets)
# counts # A bit much to actually inspect visually

#I'm not sure how what to do with the output, but this gets you a list of
#the unique vectors
unique_vectors = strsplit(names(counts), " ")
unique_vectors

num_uv <- length(unique_vectors)
# End Noam's code

# Compile unique vectors for attaching to the shapefile.
uv_df <- data.frame(do.call("cbind",unique_vectors))
colnames(uv_df) <-c(paste("uf_",1:num_uv,sep=""))
uv_df <- data.frame(geoids,uv_df)

# Load Shape
library(rgdal)
tracts_o <- readOGR(dsn=".", layer="tl_2010_06_tract10")
tracts_o <- merge(x=tracts_o, y=seeds_df, by = "GEOID10", all.x = TRUE)
tracts_o <- merge(x=tracts_o, y=uv_df, by = "GEOID10", all.x = TRUE)
writeOGR(tracts_o, ".", "seedtest4",driver="ESRI Shapefile")

>

> Here's the code I'm playing with at the moment. Basically what it does is read in a set of demographic data from csv, iterate through seed values 1:100 conducing Kmeans clustering, and saving the outputs to a list. It then implements Noam's suggestion, and appends the resulting unique vectors to the shapefile. In this case it comes up with 53 unique vectors, though quite a few are permutations of the label switch issue. Finally it joins the items together and writes it out to a shapefile.
>
> I'm not particularly elegant with my R yet, so I also welcome stylistic suggestions.
>
> Thank you,
> Nate
>
> # Load libraries
> library(psych)
> library(nFactors)
> library(plyr)
>
> #Kmeans function
> kmeanscluster <- function(seed,indf,numclus,maxiters){
>   set.seed(seed)
>   fit <- kmeans(indf, numclus,iter.max=maxiters)
>   aggregate(indf,by=list(fit$cluster),FUN=mean)
>   return(fit$cluster)
> }
>
>
> # Read in the table
> tracts <-read.table("walk_bike.csv",header=TRUE, sep=",",colClasses=c("character",rep("numeric",11)))
> # Select just the fields to use for the clustering
> natracts <-na.omit(tracts)
> wtracts <-natracts[c(2:11)]
> geoids <- natracts[c(1)]
> colnames(geoids) <- c("GEOID10")
>
> # Run Kmeans, no factor analysis
> seeds <- 1:100
> t <- lapply(seeds,kmeanscluster,indf=wtracts,4, maxiters=20)
> # Prep for join to Shapefile
> seeds_df <- data.frame(do.call("cbind",t))
> colnames(seeds_df) <-c(paste("sd_",seeds,sep=""))
> seeds_df <- data.frame(geoids,seeds_df)
>
> # Noam's code

>   uniques = unique(x)                  # This block renames the

>
> #I'm not sure how what to do with the output, but this gets you a list of

> unique_vectors = strsplit(names(counts), " ")

>

> colnames(uv_df) <-c(paste("uf_",1:num_uv,sep=""))
> uv_df <- data.frame(geoids,uv_df)
>
>
>
> # Load Shape

> tracts_o <- readOGR(dsn=".", layer="tl_2010_06_tract10")
> tracts_o <- merge(x=tracts_o, y=seeds_df, by = "GEOID10", all.x = TRUE)
> tracts_o <- merge(x=tracts_o, y=uv_df, by = "GEOID10", all.x = TRUE)

>

messages.subject: Re: CART output using party package
messages.body_plain:
Just to chime in here, I've used both rpart and ctree, and have encountered similar situations that both Rosemary and Julie mentioned. Definitely important to make sure you have no NA values in your dataset or it will likely throw out errors for MonteCarlo runs. Since the  party package uses permutation tests and statistically determines which variables are most important for use in creating splits, it is worth playing with the "maxdepth" variable, along with some of the other criteria (like relaxing significance values) when using ctree. In using rpart, I found it definitely seems to work more smoothly when you have categorical variables with many levels, but as Rosemary said, it does require significant trimming.  I found ctree easier to explain and understand once I figured out what settings seemed to make the most sense for the dataset involved.

Hello all,

The votes are in, and fall D-RUG sessions will be held Tuesdays 1:10-3 in Wickson 2124. Our first meeting will be next week, on Tuesday, Oct 7.

For those new to D-RUG, our work sessions are times for you to come to work on your own projects (including classwork) and get help on R and related topics from the D-RUG community. We have speakers every other week. These talks take up the first hour or less, leaving the rest of the time open for co-work and help.

Next week, Michael Levy <https://twitter.com/ucdlevy> will give a talk on how to use the dplyr package to make your R code easier to write and read (and faster, too!). With dplyr, you can turn this:
crime.by.state <- read.csv("CrimeStatebyState.csv")

crime.ny.2005 <- crime.by.state[crime.by.state$Year==2005 &
                                  crime.by.state$State=="New York",
                                c("Type.of.Crime", "Count")]
crime.ny.2005 <- crime.ny.2005[order(crime.ny.2005$Count,
                                     decreasing=TRUE), ]
crime.ny.2005$Proportion <- crime.ny.2005$Count /
                            sum(crime.ny.2005$Count)
summary1 <- aggregate(Count ~ Type.of.Crime,
                      data=crime.ny.2005,
                      FUN=sum)
summary2 <- aggregate(Count ~ Type.of.Crime,
                      data=crime.ny.2005,
                      FUN=length)
final <- merge(summary1, summary2,
               by="Type.of.Crime")

into this:
library(dplyr)
crime.by.state <- read.csv("CrimeStatebyState.csv")

final <- crime.by.state %>%
           filter(State=="New York", Year==2005) %>%
           arrange(desc(Count)) %>%
           select(Type.of.Crime, Count) %>%
           mutate(Proportion=Count/sum(Count)) %>%
           group_by(Type.of.Crime) %>%
           summarise(num.types = n(), counts = sum(Count))

Much better, no? Michael will show you more! See you on Tuesday.

Noam

*Thanks to Tony Fischetti for the example <http://www.onthelambda.com/2014/02/10/how-dplyr-replaced-my-most-common-r-idioms/>

> Next week, Michael Levy will give a talk on how to use the dplyr package to
> make your R code easier to write and read (and faster, too!). With dplyr,
> you can turn this:
>
> crime.by.state <- read.csv("CrimeStatebyState.csv")
>
> crime.ny.2005 <- crime.by.state[crime.by.state$Year==2005 &
>                                   crime.by.state$State=="New York",
>                                 c("Type.of.Crime", "Count")]
> crime.ny.2005 <- crime.ny.2005[order(crime.ny.2005$Count,
>                                      decreasing=TRUE), ]
> crime.ny.2005$Proportion <- crime.ny.2005$Count /
>                             sum(crime.ny.2005$Count)
> summary1 <- aggregate(Count ~ Type.of.Crime,
>                       data=crime.ny.2005,
>                       FUN=sum)
> summary2 <- aggregate(Count ~ Type.of.Crime,
>                       data=crime.ny.2005,
>                       FUN=length)
> final <- merge(summary1, summary2,
>                by="Type.of.Crime")
>
> into this:
>
> library(dplyr)
> crime.by.state <- read.csv("CrimeStatebyState.csv")
>
> final <- crime.by.state %>%
>            filter(State=="New York", Year==2005) %>%
>            arrange(desc(Count)) %>%
>            select(Type.of.Crime, Count) %>%
>            mutate(Proportion=Count/sum(Count)) %>%
>            group_by(Type.of.Crime) %>%
>            summarise(num.types = n(), counts = sum(Count))
>
